newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Uncertainty slows Russia growth-Western economist.
newsitem.headline: Uncertainty slows Russia growth-Western economist.

text.p: Russia may see some economic growth in 1997 but will be hindered by a climate of uncertainty that kept investors at bay in 1996, Western economist Richard Layard said on Monday.

"There is an unrealistic element on the side of tax collection (in the 1997 budget), which will mean that probably all the expenditure cannot be delivered," Layard, a consultant to the Russian government, told a news conference.
"This will lead to the same problem (as in 1996) of uncertainty in the budgetary sector and the problem of arrears of budgetary wages."
The State Duma lower house of parliament passed the 1997 draft budget in the first of three readings on Sunday.

Layard, whose forecasts for growth in 1997 were among the most optimistic offered by economists early this year, said 1997 would probably see growth in gross domestic product, though he declined to predict a precise level.
Sergei Pavlenko, head of the Russian Government's Centre for Economic Reform, told the same news conference that growth for the year would be flat.
"Under the best circumstances, a fall in the first half of the year will be covered in the fourth quarter, so that it is most realistic to expect zero growth for 1997," he said.
Layard said the 1997 budget was much like the 1996 budget and the next year would share many similarities.

"In a way, 1996 was lost. Many of the things that would have happened in 1996 will happen in 1997," he said, referring to disruptions by parliamentary and presidential elections as well as President Boris Yeltsin's heart bypass operation.

But he said regulatory problems, including difficulties setting up private sector companies, which he expects to lead Russia to growth, and unwillingness by local governments to give up power, were slowing growth.
"Many of the most important things are under the jurisdiction of the local governments," he said.
